items.stimulus: Marine biologist Rana Ostrow placed fragments of staghorn coral in two aquariums. The tanks received identical light, water, and nutrients, but only one also housed parrotfish, which graze on algae. After eight weeks, the coral in the parrotfish tank had grown noticeably more than the coral in the other tank. Ostrow concluded that the parrotfish helped the coral grow by keeping algae from covering and shading it.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ostrow's conclusion?
choices: The coral fragments in the parrotfish tank grew larger over eight weeks than the coral fragments in the other tank did.
Algae covered far less of the coral's surface in the parrotfish tank than it covered in the tank without parrotfish.
Both tanks received the same amount of light each day during the full eight weeks that the experiment was running.
Parrotfish can be found grazing among the corals on most healthy reefs in tropical oceans around the world.
items.explanation: Ostrow's conclusion has two parts: the parrotfish reduced the algae, and less algae let the coral grow. The passage already tells you the coral grew more. The missing link is that the parrotfish tank had less algae on the coral. Choice B shows exactly that difference between the two tanks, so it supports the proposed mechanism.

C.why: This condition was the same for both tanks, and the passage already says so. A feature the two groups share can't explain why they turned out differently, so it doesn't support the algae explanation.

D.why: You were drawn by the topic of parrotfish on reefs. Where parrotfish live in the wild doesn't show that they reduced algae on the coral in this experiment.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: The human body cannot digest dietary fiber, but certain gut bacteria break it down and release butyrate, a compound that can reduce inflammation. In a twelve-week study, one group of adults ate a high-fiber diet while a second, otherwise similar group ate a low-fiber diet. By the end of the study, the high-fiber group had lower levels of inflammation markers in the blood. The researchers concluded that this difference arose because the high-fiber diet increased butyrate production.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' conclusion?
choices: Adults in the high-fiber group had lower levels of inflammation markers in the blood than adults in the low-fiber group did.
Adults in the high-fiber group had higher levels of butyrate in the digestive tract than adults in the low-fiber group did.
Adults in both groups ate about the same number of calories each day during the twelve weeks that the study lasted.
Adults in the low-fiber group had higher levels of butyrate in the digestive tract than adults in the high-fiber group did.
items.explanation: The proposed chain runs from more fiber to more butyrate to less inflammation. The passage already reports less inflammation, so the claim depends on the middle link: the high-fiber group must have produced more butyrate. Choice B shows that difference, in the right direction.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. You chose a restatement of the result the passage already reports. It doesn't mention butyrate, so it can't support the claim that butyrate caused the difference.

C.why: Calorie intake was the same for both groups, so it can't separate them. It also says nothing about butyrate, the mechanism the conclusion proposes.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: A moderate earthquake recently struck a region where a river valley lies next to a rocky ridge. Both areas are about 30 kilometers from the epicenter. Homes in the valley sit on loose river sediment, while homes on the ridge sit on solid bedrock. Although homes in the two areas are built in similar ways, the valley homes suffered far more cracking. A team of seismologists concluded that the valley's sediment amplified the ground shaking, which caused the greater damage.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the seismologists' conclusion?
choices: Homes in the valley showed much more cracking after the earthquake than homes on the nearby ridge showed.
Instruments in the valley recorded stronger ground shaking during the earthquake than instruments on the ridge did.
The valley and the ridge were each located about the same distance from the epicenter of the earthquake.
Earthquakes in the region have occurred beneath the valley more often than they have occurred beneath the ridge.
items.explanation: The seismologists claim the sediment made the shaking stronger and that stronger shaking caused more damage. The damage is already known. What still needs showing is that the shaking really was stronger in the valley than on the ridge. Choice B gives that measurement and separates the two areas.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. You picked the observed result, the extra cracking, which the passage already states. It doesn't show that the shaking was stronger, so it adds no support for the amplification explanation.

C.why: The two areas share this distance, and the passage already says so. A feature common to both can't explain why they suffered different damage.

D.why: This concerns where earthquakes start over time, not how one earthquake's shaking differed between the two areas. Treating it as evidence of amplification goes beyond what the finding shows.

items.stimulus: Alder Creek and Birch Creek drain neighboring watersheds of nearly equal size and steepness. Three years ago, wetlands were restored along the upper reaches of Alder Creek, while the wetlands along Birch Creek remained drained. During a recent heavy storm, Birch Creek overflowed its banks, but Alder Creek did not. Hydrologists concluded that the restored wetlands held back much of the rainwater and released it slowly, keeping Alder Creek's flow below flood level.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hydrologists' conclusion?
choices: Birch Creek overflowed its banks during the heavy storm, while Alder Creek stayed within its banks the whole time.
The restored wetlands along Alder Creek filled with water during the storm and drained gradually over several days.
Both Alder Creek and Birch Creek usually carry more water in the spring than they carry in late summer each year.
Birch Creek's drained wetlands held back more of the storm's rainwater than Alder Creek's restored wetlands did.
items.explanation: The conclusion names a specific mechanism: the wetlands stored the rain and released it slowly. Choice B shows the restored wetlands doing exactly that during this storm, which links the restoration to the creek staying below flood level.

C.why: This seasonal pattern is true of both creeks, so it can't explain why only Birch Creek flooded. It also doesn't involve the wetlands at all.

items.stimulus: At high altitude the air holds less oxygen, which can prompt the body to make more red blood cells, the cells that carry oxygen to working muscles. Sports scientist Tomasz Rehberg recruited 40 cyclists. For six weeks, half trained at a mountain camp and half trained at sea level, and both groups did identical workouts. Rehberg hypothesizes that the mountain group's red blood cell counts will increase but the sea-level group's will not.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Rehberg's hypothesis?
choices: The red blood cell counts of cyclists in both groups rose by similar amounts over the six weeks of training.
The red blood cell counts of cyclists in the mountain group rose, while those in the sea-level group stayed about the same.
Cyclists in the mountain group said their workouts felt harder than cyclists in the sea-level group said theirs did.
The red blood cell counts of cyclists in the sea-level group rose, while those in the mountain group stayed about the same.
items.explanation: The hypothesis has two parts: the mountain group's counts go up, and the sea-level group's do not. Choice B confirms both, so it separates the two groups exactly as the hypothesis predicts.

A.why: You picked a finding that is true of both groups equally. If both counts rose, the result does not separate mountain training from sea-level training, and the hypothesis says only one group's counts should rise.

C.why: You matched the topic, not the claim. How hard the workouts felt is not the red blood cell counts the hypothesis is about.

D.why: You reversed the groups. The hypothesis expects the mountain group's counts to rise, not the sea-level group's.

items.stimulus: In a forest, soil and roots soak up much of the rain that falls. When the trees are cleared, more of that rain runs quickly over the ground into streams. She concluded that logging speeds up runoff, so the logged watershed's stream peaks sooner after rain begins.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's conclusion?
choices: Streamflow in the forested watershed peaked about two hours after rain began, compared with six hours in the logged watershed.
The logged watershed had much less tree cover and much more bare ground than the neighboring forested watershed had.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Astronomer Ines Carvalho's team used a space telescope to survey 40 rocky planets orbiting red dwarf stars. Planets around slowly rotating stars were far more likely to show signs of an atmosphere than planets around rapidly rotating ones. Because rapidly rotating red dwarfs typically emit frequent ultraviolet flares, the team concluded that flare activity, not rotation itself, explains the pattern: repeated flares strip atmospheres away, whereas the calmer slow rotators allow atmospheres to persist.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's conclusion?
choices: The few rapidly rotating stars in the sample that seldom flared hosted planets with atmospheres about as often as the slowly rotating stars did.
Planets orbiting slowly rotating stars showed atmospheric signatures roughly three times as often as planets orbiting rapidly rotating stars did.
Around both kinds of star, planets on wider orbits were likelier to show atmospheres than planets on closer orbits, and by similar margins.
The rapidly rotating stars in the sample flared less often than the slowly rotating stars did, although their individual flares were brighter.
items.explanation: The team says flares, not rotation, are the cause. To support that, a finding has to pull the two apart. Fast rotators that rarely flare have planets with atmospheres at the slow-rotator rate, so when flares are absent, fast rotation alone doesn't cost planets their atmospheres. That points to flares.

B.why: You picked a restatement of the pattern the team is explaining. Putting a number on how much slow rotators differ doesn't show whether flares or rotation is responsible.

C.why: You picked a pattern that holds equally around both kinds of star. Orbital distance has nothing to do with flares and doesn't separate the two groups.

items.stimulus: In the fall of 2023, a county health department texted flu-shot reminders to residents of two similar towns. items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: In the 1830s, handloom weavers in two neighboring towns obtained yarn in different ways. In Brennick, most bought it on credit from a single merchant who also purchased their finished cloth; in Tessel, most paid cash for yarn at an open market. Over the decade, Brennick's cloth became far more uniform in width and color than Tessel's. Historian Ada Lindqvist argues that the credit arrangement produced this difference by letting the merchant dictate standards that weavers had to meet.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's claim?
choices: Cloth from both Brennick and Tessel sold at noticeably higher prices at the end of the decade than it had at the start of the decade.
Tessel's market officials enforced standard widths for all cloth sold there, while the Brennick merchant accepted cloth of any width.
The Brennick merchant's ledgers record refusing pieces that missed set widths, while Tessel's market records show no pieces turned away.
By the end of the decade, Brennick's cloth was much closer to a single standard width than Tessel's cloth was, judging by surviving samples.
items.explanation: Lindqvist's claim is a chain: credit gave the merchant control, the merchant used that control to set standards, and the standards made the cloth uniform. Choice C supplies the middle link for Brennick, where the merchant rejected pieces that missed the standard, and shows that Tessel had no such pressure. That explains why the two towns differed.

B.why: This reverses the claim. It puts the enforced standards in Tessel and takes them away from the Brennick merchant, which would undercut the idea that the merchant's control produced the uniformity.

D.why: This only restates the observed result, that Brennick's cloth was more uniform. It doesn't show that the credit arrangement or the merchant's standards caused it.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: In 1892 a publisher issued an inexpensive songbook containing forty of the ballads then sung in a rural region, with each melody printed in notation. When folklorists recorded singers there in the 1920s, they found far fewer melodic variants of the songbook ballads than of ballads the book had omitted. Musicologist Tomás Ferreira argues that the printed notation itself slowed the melodies' drift, and that the gap does not simply reflect which ballads were most popular.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's claim?
choices: Before 1892, the ballads chosen for the songbook were already sung far more widely in the region than the ballads that it omitted.
Recordings from the 1920s include far fewer melodic variants of the songbook ballads than of the ballads that the songbook omitted.
Ballads in both groups had more melodic variants in the 1920s recordings than in transcriptions made in the region in the 1880s.
Among ballads equally widely sung before 1892, those in the songbook had far fewer variants by the 1920s than those it omitted.
items.explanation: Ferreira's claim has two parts: printing slowed the drift, and popularity does not explain the gap. To support both, a finding has to hold popularity constant and still show the difference. Choice D compares ballads that were equally popular, and the printed ones still had fewer variants. That points to the notation as the cause.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: In a Norwegian fjord, common periwinkles from a sheltered inner site have shells about 30 percent thicker than periwinkles from an outer site near the fjord's mouth. The water at the inner site averages about 3°C warmer, and shore crabs, which crush periwinkles, are far more abundant there. In many mollusks, warmer water speeds shell deposition, so the difference could simply be a by-product of temperature. Marine biologist Sigrun Aasen and colleagues, however, concluded that the periwinkles thicken their shells in response to chemical cues released by crabs, not because of the warmer water.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' conclusion?
choices: Surveys over several years found that inner-site periwinkles consistently had thicker shells and lived among more crabs than outer-site periwinkles did.
Outer-site periwinkles kept in crab-free tanks grew thicker shells when their water was warmed to the inner site's temperature than when it was not.
Outer-site periwinkles kept in tanks at the outer site's temperature grew thicker shells when given water that had held crabs than when given crab-free water.
Periwinkles taken from the outer site and caged at the inner site grew shells as thick as those of inner-site periwinkles within a single year.
items.explanation: The conclusion has two parts: crab cues cause the thickening, and warmth does not. To support both, a finding has to vary the crab cue while holding temperature fixed. Choice C does exactly that. Outer-site snails were kept at the colder outer-site temperature, and the only difference between the two groups was whether their water had held crabs. The cue group still grew thicker shells, so the cue alone produced the effect without any extra warmth.

A.why: This just restates the observation the passage starts with: thick shells and many crabs at the inner site. The researchers' explanation and the temperature explanation both predict this pattern, so it can't help you choose between them. You picked a finding that repeats the result instead of isolating its cause.

B.why: Here warmth alone, with no crabs, thickened the shells. That supports the alternative the researchers rejected, so it weakens their conclusion. You probably saw a controlled tank experiment with thicker shells and missed which variable was changed.

D.why: This is the trap for students who already know they need an experiment. Moving the snails to the inner site exposes them to more crabs and to warmer water at the same time. Their shells would thicken under either explanation, so the result can't show that crabs rather than temperature are responsible. You read support for one cause into a result that two causes explain equally well.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: On dairy farms in western Ireland, barn swallow pairs nesting in barns that house cattle fledge more chicks per brood than pairs nesting in barns left empty. Cattle barns differ from empty ones in two relevant ways. Dung and animals attract large numbers of flies, a staple of nestling diets, and the cattle's body heat keeps the air several degrees warmer. items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: When fly traps cut fly numbers in cattle barns but left air temperature unchanged, both parents' feeding rates and fledging success fell toward empty-barn levels.
Within cattle barns, pairs that made more feeding trips per hour went on to fledge more chicks than did pairs in those barns that made fewer trips.
Throughout the nesting season, cattle barns held both far more flies and noticeably warmer air than did the empty barns on the same farms.
Parents in cattle barns and in empty barns made feeding trips at similar rates, but chicks in cattle barns lost less weight on cold nights.
items.explanation: Break the hypothesis into a chain and a rival. The chain runs from flies to more frequent feeding to more fledglings. The rival, warmth, is said not to be the cause. You confirmed one link of the chain and treated it as support for the whole hypothesis.

D.why: Similar feeding rates break the middle link the researchers depend on. Chicks staying heavier on cold nights points to warmth instead. This finding weakens the hypothesis. You may have noticed that cattle-barn chicks did better and missed which cause that benefit points to.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Compression tights are widely thought to speed recovery between bouts of running by boosting circulation in the legs. In trials at her lab, runners wearing the tights did recover faster between repeated hill sprints than runners wearing loose shorts. Sports physiologist Noor Haddad suspects, however, that circulation is not the cause. She hypothesizes that the tights help by damping the vibration of the thigh muscles each time the foot strikes the ground, which limits the small-scale tissue damage that repeated impact produces.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haddad's hypothesis?
choices: Runners wearing the tights recovered faster between hill sprints than runners wearing loose shorts of the same weight did.
Blood flow in the thigh muscles was about 15 percent higher in runners wearing the tights than in runners wearing loose shorts.
In cyclists, whose legs take almost no impact, the tights raised thigh blood flow as much as in runners but did not speed recovery.
Runners wearing the tights recovered faster and, according to motion sensors, had less thigh vibration at each foot strike.
items.explanation: Haddad's hypothesis has two parts: damping vibration from impact is what helps, and better circulation is not. To support it, a finding has to pull the two apart. Cyclists' legs take almost no impact, so the tights have no vibration to damp. They still raise blood flow just as much, yet recovery doesn't improve. Circulation alone isn't enough to produce the benefit, which points to impact damping.

A.why: You chose the observed result, which the passage already reports. It shows that the tights help but says nothing about why, so it can't favour vibration over circulation.

B.why: You picked a finding about circulation, the explanation Haddad rejects. Higher blood flow fits the common view at least as well as hers, and nothing here links the benefit to vibration.

D.why: You saw the right mechanism and stopped. In these runners the tights also boost circulation, so less vibration and faster recovery happen together with higher blood flow. The finding can't tell which one caused the faster recovery.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Streams with beaver dams often keep flowing through late summer, when nearby undammed streams run dry. One explanation is that the ponds behind the dams store surface water and release it slowly. Hydrologist Elena Sokolova proposes a different route: by spreading water across the floodplain, the dams raise the local water table, and groundwater then seeps back into the channel below the dam for weeks after inflow stops. Her team concluded that this groundwater pathway, not pond storage, is what sustains the late-summer flow.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's conclusion?
choices: In August, dammed streams were still flowing at most survey points, whereas nearby undammed streams had stopped flowing entirely.
Below dams whose ponds had already drained by August, flow continued wherever floodplain wells showed the water table was still raised.
Ponds behind the dams held more water in early July than the streams below them carried over the whole month of August.
Floodplain water tables stood higher along dammed streams than undammed ones, and the dams' ponds stayed full well into August.
items.explanation: The conclusion makes two claims: groundwater sustains the flow, and pond storage does not. Once a pond has drained, it has no stored water left to release, so pond storage can't explain flow below it. If flow continues there, and only where the water table is still raised, the flow is tied to groundwater and the rival explanation is removed.

A.why: You chose a restatement of the observed difference between dammed and undammed streams. Both explanations predict this result, so it can't favour one.

C.why: You chose evidence that the ponds hold enough water to supply August flow. That supports pond storage, the explanation the team rejects.

D.why: You noticed the raised water table but missed that full ponds were present too. With both possible sources in place, this finding can't show which one keeps the stream flowing.

items.stimulus: Engineers sometimes embed capsules of dormant bacterial spores in concrete. When a crack lets in water, the spores revive and precipitate calcium carbonate, which seals the crack. Larvae of both exposed and unexposed parents grew more slowly in acidified water than they did in normal seawater.

items.explanation: The conclusion has two parts. C.why: You chose a result that holds for both groups of larvae. It shows that acidification slows growth but doesn't compare offspring of exposed and unexposed parents.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Wheat planted along hedgerows often outyields wheat in the open centers of the same fields. Hedgerows slow the wind, which reduces water loss from the crop's leaves. They also house parasitoid wasps that lay eggs in aphids, killing these sap-feeding pests before their numbers build. Agronomist Priya Raman concluded that the yield gain in her study fields came chiefly from the wasps' suppression of aphids rather than from shelter from the wind.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Raman's conclusion?
choices: Wheat growing beside the hedgerows yielded more grain per hectare than wheat growing in the open centers of the fields.
Wind speeds over wheat beside the hedgerows were lower than wind speeds over wheat growing in the field centers.
Hedgerows netted so that wasps could not reach the wheat still cut wind speed over the adjacent wheat by about half.
Beside hedgerows netted so that wasps could not reach the wheat, the wheat yielded no more than wheat in the field centers.
items.explanation: Raman credits the wasps rather than the windbreak, so the evidence has to remove one and keep the other. Netting keeps the wasps out while the hedgerow still blocks wind. If the yield gain disappears under those conditions, wind shelter alone doesn't produce it, and the wasps do.

A.why: You chose the observed yield gain, which the passage already reports. Both explanations predict it, so it doesn't favour Raman's.

B.why: You chose evidence for the wind-shelter mechanism, the one Raman downplays. Calmer air near hedgerows fits the rival explanation, not hers.

C.why: You recognised the right experiment but chose its setup instead of its result. Knowing that netted hedgerows still block wind tells you nothing until you know what happened to the yield.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Probate inventories from the Lowland towns show that the share of households owning printed cotton rose sharply in the 1780s, displacing woolen worsted. Many historians attribute the change to fashion, spread by illustrated magazines that praised light printed fabrics. Historian Margit Svensson argues instead that the decisive factor was price: a canal opened in 1779 cut the cost of shipping cotton cloth to towns along its route.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Svensson's claim?
choices: Printed cotton ownership rose in the 1780s in canal towns but stayed flat in nearby towns off the canal where the magazines circulated equally.
In canal towns, printed cotton cost less in the 1780s than in the 1770s, and magazines praising it were widely read there as well.
Magazines praising printed fabrics reached canal towns and towns off the canal in roughly equal numbers during the 1780s.
By 1790, inventories in the Lowland towns listed printed cotton in more households than they listed woolen worsted.
items.explanation: Svensson's claim holds only if the canal's price cut, not fashion, explains the rise. The towns off the canal had the same magazines but not the cheaper shipping. If ownership rose only in canal towns, fashion alone wasn't enough, and the cost difference accounts for the change.

B.why: You saw the price drop, which is Svensson's factor. But the magazines were also widely read in those same towns, so the finding can't show which one drove the change.

C.why: You chose a fact that is equally true of both kinds of town and gives no ownership figures. Without knowing what people bought, it can't link the rise to price.

D.why: You chose a restatement of the observed shift from worsted to cotton. Both explanations predict it, so it adds no support for Svensson.
